clips.name: park_joy
clips.note: Hand-held pan across a park, water spray and foliage. The hardest kind of content to code: motion in every direction and no flat area to hide in.

clips.name: blue_sky
clips.note: A rotating shot of bare branches against an open sky. Large smooth gradients next to hard thin edges: the classic banding trap.

prose.av1_low_why: Below about 0.035 bits per pixel per frame: 1080p30 under 2 Mbit/s, or 4K60 under 17 Mbit/s. AV1's lead is largest here, 47.3% under H.264 at VMAF 80 with SVT-AV1 and 46.6% with libaom on this corpus. This is where 4K streaming actually lives, so “what wins at 4K” and “what wins when bits are scarce” are the same question. Use the SVT encoder: same bitstream, same decoder, a fraction of the CPU.
prose.av1_mid_why: Still first among the codecs anything can decode at ordinary streaming density: 40.2% under H.264 at VMAF 90 with SVT-AV1 and 41.3% with libaom. Royalty-free, in every current browser, and decoded in silicon on 2023-and-later phones and most smart TVs. The cost is on the encode side, and which encoder you pick moves it by 3.6 times.
prose.mid_tier2_why: These two are the same codec generation and it shows: VP9 is only 4.2% ahead at VMAF 90, averaged over the three resolutions, and it never gets further than 7.6 percentage points ahead anywhere. Pick on reach, not on efficiency. VP9 plays in every browser and costs nothing to licence; HEVC does neither, and has hardware everywhere.
prose.vp9_high_why: At this density the two tier-2 codecs are close enough that efficiency stops deciding: VP9 is 3.1% smaller than HEVC at VMAF 95, and both are well behind AV1. So pick on where the file has to play. HEVC is what broadcast chains, UHD Blu-ray, Apple devices and cameras speak natively; VP9 is what browsers speak. If it is going to a television, that is HEVC.
prose.low_tier2_why: Where AV1 is not an option, this is the next best thing anything can decode when bits are scarce: 15.5% smaller than H.264 at VMAF 80, against 8.6% smaller for the other one. VP9 carries no licence bill and plays in every browser, which is why it takes this square even when the margin over HEVC is small.
prose.converge_note: the best saving against H.264 falls from 55.9% at VMAF 80 to 45.0% at VMAF 95, and the gap between the five non-H.264 encoders closes from 47.2 to 43.1 percentage points
prose.ranking_note: The ordering at VMAF 90 is VVC then AV1 (libaom) then AV1 (SVT) then VP9 then HEVC then H.264, and it is that same ordering at every resolution and every target measured bar a few. The exceptions: VVC then AV1 (libaom) then AV1 (SVT) then VP9 then H.264 then HEVC at 720p VMAF 95; VVC then AV1 (SVT) then AV1 (libaom) then VP9 then H.264 then HEVC at 540p VMAF 95, 540p VMAF 93, 540p VMAF 90; VVC then AV1 (SVT) then AV1 (libaom) then VP9 then HEVC then H.264 at 540p VMAF 85, 540p VMAF 80. The margins are another matter. VVC is 52.1% under H.264 at 1080p and 47.3% at 540p; HEVC is 10.5% and -1.2%. The largest swing across resolutions for one codec at one target is 14.9 percentage points (HEVC). Resolution does not reorder the codecs; it decides how much the newer ones are worth, and it points the same way as bitrate does.
prose.claim_hypothesis: Half right, and the half that is right is more useful than it looks. The ranking does not move much: VVC then AV1 (libaom) then AV1 (SVT) then VP9 then HEVC then H.264 at 1080p, and the same order almost everywhere else, so HEVC does not win at 1080p between 1 and 10 Mbit/s. VVC does, by 52.1% against H.264 where HEVC manages 10.5%, and among the codecs a real audience can decode it is AV1 at 44.4%. But the intuition that resolution matters is correct, just not in the way the question assumed: it changes the size of the win, not its owner. AV1's lead over H.264 goes from 39.6% at 540p to 44.4% at 1080p, and HEVC's from -1.2% to 10.5%: at 540p HEVC is barely worth the trouble. Extrapolate the trend and 4K is where the modern codecs are furthest ahead, for two reasons at once. More pixels gives their larger transforms and prediction blocks more to work with, and 4K at a normal streaming bitrate sits further left on the bits-per-pixel axis, where their lead is largest anyway. 4K60 at 15 Mbit/s is 0.0301 bits per pixel per frame; 1080p30 at 3 Mbit/s is 0.0482.
prose.lede: Normalise the bitrate to bits per pixel per frame and the question becomes answerable. VVC produced the smallest file at 540p, 720p and 1080p at every quality target measured, and AV1 came first among the codecs a real audience can decode. What moves is how much the winner wins by: the lead grows with resolution, and grows again as bits get scarce. That is exactly the corner 4K streaming sits in.
prose.savings_lede: Three bars per encoder, one per resolution. If the best codec really changed with resolution, the groups would reorder. They do not: VVC is first at all three, and AV1 first among the deployable ones. What changes is the length of the bars, and it changes a lot. That is the answer to the hypothesis, and it is not the answer the hypothesis expected.
prose.collapse_note: Three curves, one shape, and a real offset between them. At 0.04 bits per pixel per frame AV1 (libaom) reaches VMAF 89.7 at 1080p and 82.7 at 540p, a gap of 7.0 points for the same bits per pixel. Higher resolution is cheaper per pixel, because neighbouring pixels are more alike and prediction has more to work with. So normalising by pixel rate puts the resolutions on one axis, not on one line, and what it buys is that the ordering of the codecs and the shape of every curve become directly comparable across them.
prose.cost_note: At matched VMAF 93 and 1080p, VVC costs 37.8 times what H.264 costs to encode, libaom-AV1 6.5 times, VP9 3.4 times, HEVC 1.9 times and SVT-AV1 1.8 times. Two things follow. The spread between the cheapest and the dearest is a factor of 38, so for anything watched once the encode can easily cost more than the bandwidth it saves, and for anything watched a million times it is free. And the choice of encoder inside one format moves the bill as much as the choice of format does: the two AV1 rows here are the same bitstream, 3.6 times apart in CPU. That, and not compression efficiency, is why live streaming still ships H.264 while catalogue video has moved on.
prose.metric_note: The three metrics disagree, as they always do: at VMAF 90 the largest gap between VMAF's verdict and another metric's is 24.5 percentage points (VP9 scored with SSIM), and the ordering is not identical under all three, so the table is the honest summary and the headline percentages should be read as VMAF's opinion. SSIM is a poor cross-codec judge at low rates and that is where most of the disagreement sits. VMAF's own weaknesses run the other way: it over-rewards sharpening and is weak on banding.
prose.claim_hevc50: Not on these measurements, and not close. Against x264 at the same preset and the same VMAF, x265 came in 10.5% smaller at 1080p and VMAF 90; its best showing anywhere was 16.9% smaller at 1080p and VMAF 80; and at 540p it was 1.2% larger than x264 for the same picture. The 50% figure traces back to Ohm, Sullivan, Tan and Wiegand's 2012 comparison, which measured the HEVC and H.264 reference encoders under subjective testing. Two things shrink it in practice: x264 is a far better H.264 encoder than the reference software was, and PSNR-driven reference comparisons flatter the newer codec. That second point shows up directly in this sweep: score the identical encodes with PSNR-Y instead of VMAF and x265 comes out 23.8% smaller than x264 rather than 10.5% smaller. A good part of the distance between 50% and what you will actually see is the choice of metric. Twenty to thirty percent is the number to plan with at 1080p, and less than that below it.

v_vp9_class.text: Right about close, wrong about the crossover

prose.claim_vp9: The 'very equal' half is right and it is the important half: across every resolution and every target measured, VP9 and HEVC are within 7.6 percentage points of each other, and at VMAF 90 the gap is 4.2%. There is no crossover on this corpus: VP9 is ahead at both ends, by 7.6% at VMAF 80 and 3.1% at VMAF 95. It is a real edge to VP9 and it is a small one. They are the same codec generation, they were finished within a year of each other, and the reason YouTube ships VP9 is that it is royalty-free and plays in Chrome, not that it compresses better. For scale: AV1 files are 35.1% smaller than VP9 files at VMAF 90 for the same picture, encoded with SVT-AV1. That gap is worth choosing on; four percent is not.
prose.claim_av1: This has it exactly backwards, and it is the most common misconception about AV1. Decoding AV1 is a little more expensive than decoding HEVC and is comfortably within a software decoder on any modern CPU; dav1d decodes 1080p faster than real time on a phone core. Hardware decode is now in every 2023-and-later flagship SoC, most smart TVs, and every GPU from RTX 30, RDNA 2 and Intel Arc onward. It is the encode side that costs, and even there it depends entirely on which encoder you mean. On this corpus libaom needed 6.5 times H.264's CPU for the same VMAF; SVT-AV1 needed 1.8 times, which is less than what x265 costs, for a file 37.8% smaller than x265's. The hardware you want for AV1 is on the encoder, and most people never touch that side.
prose.av1_encoders_note: libaom is the reference encoder and it is slow on purpose. SVT-AV1 is what production pipelines actually run, and this sweep now has both. At matched VMAF 93 and 1080p, libaom cost 0.69 CPU seconds per frame and SVT-AV1 0.19, a factor of 3.6. At VMAF 90 SVT-AV1's files came out 1.8% larger than libaom's, averaged over the three resolutions, so the speed costs a few percent of efficiency and no more. The mean hides a split worth knowing: SVT-AV1 is 3.9% larger than libaom at 1080p and 2.6% smaller at 540p, and the gap against it is widest at the high-quality end (7.1% larger at 1080p and VMAF 95). Either way the page's old caveat holds and it was a large one: the libaom bar is the price of the reference encoder, not the price of the format. Production runs SVT, and on this corpus that trades 1.8% of bitrate on average for 3.6 times the CPU back.
prose.vvc_map_why: Now measured, not cited. At VMAF 90 libvvenc produced files 47.2% smaller than x265's and 14.9% smaller than SVT-AV1's, averaged over the three resolutions, for 38 times H.264's encode CPU. It is on the map at the top because the y-axis is decoder reach and VVC has none: no browser, no phone, no GPU. The blocker is patent licensing, not compute, which is the same thing that held HEVC back for a decade.
prose.vvc_efficiency: On this corpus VVC is the smallest file at every resolution and every target measured. At VMAF 90, averaged over the three resolutions, it is 49.1% smaller than x264, 47.2% smaller than x265, 14.9% smaller than SVT-AV1 and 13.5% smaller than libaom-AV1. So it beats both AV1 encoders here, which is the direction the literature predicts, though not by the margin the literature reports.
prose.vvc_cost: It is the most expensive thing here by a wide margin: 4.01 CPU seconds per 1080p frame at matched VMAF 93, against 0.19 for SVT-AV1 and 0.11 for x264. That is 38 times H.264 and 21 times SVT-AV1. libvvenc is young and will get faster, but at -preset medium today the compression it buys costs real money to produce.
prose.vvc_vs_lit: Published work (Nguyen and Marpe 2021) puts the VVC reference encoder about 36 to 37% under the HEVC reference encoder under JVET common test conditions, and AV1 only 10 to 15% under the same baseline. This sweep measures 47.2% smaller against x265 and puts AV1 much closer to VVC than that. Four things differ and all of them matter: the encoders (libvvenc and x265 against reference software), the presets, three seconds of two hard clips against the JVET test set, and VMAF against PSNR-based BD-rate. A result measured this way is not a correction to that work; it is a different question, answered with the encoders people can actually run.
prose.claim_vvc: It is Versatile Video Coding, H.266, and there is no “1” in it. The technical claim holds and this page can now say so from its own measurements rather than from a citation: at VMAF 90 libvvenc's files were 47.2% smaller than x265's and 14.9% smaller than SVT-AV1's on this corpus. The advanced part is real. The availability is not: no browser decodes it, no phone decodes it, and the encode cost at -preset medium is 38 times H.264's. Advanced and unusable are not the same claim. See the VVC section above.
prose.method_corpus: Two pristine uncompressed clips from the Xiph derf collection: park_joy (high motion, 3 s, 150 frames at 50 fps); blue_sky (flat gradient, 3 s, 75 frames at 25 fps). Each was fetched as raw 1080p y4m and downscaled with Lanczos to 720p and 540p; nothing was ever upscaled. Every clip was swept on its own CRF ladder in six encoders at three resolutions, 267 encodes in total, 6.0 CPU-hours of encoding and 0.5 CPU-hours of scoring.
prose.method_metric: Quality was scored with VMAF (model vmaf_v0.6.1) through ffmpeg's libvmaf filter, with PSNR-Y and SSIM recorded in the same pass. Each codec was swept on its own CRF ladder; the rate at a given VMAF target was found by interpolating that codec's own curve per clip, then taking the geometric mean across clips. CRF ladders are per clip, because a single ladder placed to span VMAF 78 to 98 on the high-motion clip only reaches the top of the range on the easy one, and the comparison at the low end would then be an artefact of the sweep. Rate is always bits per pixel per frame; container overhead is removed, so an IVF frame header is not counted against VP9 and AV1, and the H.264, HEVC and VVC streams are raw Annex-B with no container at all. Encoders: libx264, libx265, libvpx-vp9, libaom-av1, libsvtav1 and libvvenc, each pinned to a single thread so encoder CPU time is a clean cost measure.
prose.method_binary: Every row was produced by one ffmpeg build, a GPL build carrying libvvenc and libsvtav1 alongside the four older encoders. That matters more than it sounds: an earlier version of this page used a static ffmpeg 7.0.2 that had no VVC encoder and no SVT-AV1, so VVC was cited from the literature and AV1 was represented only by the slow reference encoder. Adding two encoders from a new binary while keeping the old rows would have made part of the comparison a statement about which build produced which codec, so the whole sweep was re-run: all 267 encodes here come from the same binary, the same clips and the same ladder method. The previous sweep is kept in the repository as rd_video_ffmpeg702.jsonl and none of its rows are mixed in. It was worth doing. Comparing the 42 settings that appear in both files, at identical CRF on identical sources, x264 came out byte-for-byte the same size, x265 and VP9 within about a percent, and libaom-AV1 24% smaller for the same picture. Almost the whole difference between this page's AV1 figures and its previous ones is that one encoder getting better, not a change of method.
prose.caveat_presets: x264 and x265 ran at -preset medium, VP9 at -cpu-used 2, libaom-AV1 at -cpu-used 6, SVT-AV1 at -preset 6 and libvvenc at -preset medium. The four older settings are unchanged from the previous sweep so the page stays comparable with what it said before. SVT-AV1 preset 6 is the encoder's own VOD recommendation and it landed within 6% of x265 -preset medium's cost per frame here, so it is a like-for-like speed choice rather than a favour to AV1. libvvenc medium is the middle of its five presets and its default; faster was the fallback if the time budget had not held, and it would have understated VVC. Slower presets are worth several percent of BD-rate and they are worth most to the codecs with the largest search spaces, so these settings understate HEVC, AV1 and VVC rather than overstate them.
prose.caveat_vmaf: VMAF was trained on Netflix's own catalogue and its own scaling pipeline. It over-rewards sharpening and contrast enhancement, it is weak on banding, and it was fitted for 1080p viewed at a set distance. PSNR-Y and SSIM are recorded alongside every encode in the raw data, and the cross-check above shows they do not simply agree: PSNR-Y is markedly more generous to the newer codecs than VMAF is, SSIM markedly less. Where a page quotes one number, it is quoting one metric's opinion. Everything here is VMAF's.
prose.caveat_corpus: Two clips is a small corpus, and it is deliberately a hard one: the high-motion clip is close to the worst case for any codec, and the flat-gradient clip is the banding worst case. Real catalogue content is easier than both, so the absolute bits-per-pixel numbers here are pessimistic. Two of the six encoders here, libaom and libvvenc, are slow enough that the corpus size is a compute decision; a third clip is fetched by the corpus script and is in the repository, but was not swept (in_to_tree), so it backs no number on this page rather than half-backing several. The direction of every finding is robust to corpus size; the exact percentages are not general constants.
prose.crf_note: Those are ranges because content difficulty moves CRF a long way. On this corpus the high-motion clip and the flat-gradient clip needed x264 CRF 25 and 32 respectively to land on the same VMAF 93: the same setting is a different picture on different footage, which is why per-title encoding exists.
